QF.id: IV Clearing Settlement and Risk Management_46

question.text: A clearing member has a total margin requirement of Rs. 1 crore. They have deposited Rs. 40 lakhs in cash and Rs. 60 lakhs in Government Securities (gross of haircut). Ignoring haircut, is their margin composition compliant with the 50% cash-equivalent rule?

answer.text: No, because only 40% is in cash/cash equivalents, which is below the required 50% minimum
Yes, because the total deposited (Rs. 1 crore) meets the total requirement
Yes, because Government Securities are classified as cash equivalents
No, because G-Secs are not accepted as margin collateral

explanation.text: The Logic: Per the workbook, Government of India Securities are classified under the cash component / cash equivalents, alongside cash, bank FDRs, bank guarantees, money market mutual fund units, gilt funds and sovereign gold bonds. So both Rs. 40 lakhs in cash and Rs. 60 lakhs in G-Secs (gross of haircut) count toward the cash-equivalent component, giving 100% cash-equivalent composition - well above the 50% floor. The Trap: The common misconception is to treat G-Secs as non-cash collateral. The 50% rule applies to the cash component (which includes G-Secs); only approved equities / certain non-government securities sit outside this component. Note: Pages 257-259 and 268 list G-Secs in the cash component / cash equivalents subject to haircut. In practice, applicable haircuts can reduce the effective cash-equivalent value, so a member running close to 50% should verify the post-haircut figure.
